q: Why is Kadlekai Parishe a thing?
a: Basavanagudi's Bull Temple sits on what used to be groundnut country. The story goes that a bull would wreck the crop until farmers offered the first harvest at Dodda Basavana Gudi - and the animal stopped. Kadlekai Parishe is still that offering: when the new groundnut comes in (Karthika, usually Nov/Dec), farmers pile it around the temple, and the streets turn into a fair of roasted kadlekai, clay toys and bangles. It is a harvest thanksgiving that the city grew around, not a tourist calendar invention.

q: Is Bengaluru actually named after boiled beans?
a: The folk tale is charming: a Hoysala king is served boiled beans (benda kaalu) by an old woman, and names the place Benda-kaalu-ooru. Inscriptions are less romantic. A 9th-century stone at Begur already records Benguluru, centuries before that story is told. Keep the beans as a story people like; the name is older than the anecdote.

q: Why are the spiced peanuts called Congress kadlekai?
a: Iyengar bakeries' masala peanuts took the name after the 1969 split in the Indian National Congress - two factions, two colours of spice mix in one packet. It stuck as a joke you can still eat with a khara bun.

q: Why does Bengaluru Karaga stop at a dargah?
a: On the main night, the Karaga procession from Dharmaraya Swamy Temple pauses at the Hazrat Tawakkal Mastan dargah in Cottonpet. The stop is not a modern interfaith photo-op; it has been part of the route since the 18th century, when a Sufi saint is said to have blessed the festival. The city's oldest living festival still walks that agreement.

q: Why the two-metal-cup filter coffee set?
a: The tumbler and the wide dabara are a cooling kit. You pour back and forth so the decoction-and-milk mix drops from scalding to drinkable without watering it down. The stretch of coffee between the two cups is the point, not a flourish for photographs.

q: Why is Bengaluru milder than the rest of the south?
a: The city sits on the Deccan plateau at about 900 metres (roughly 3,000 ft). That height, not sea breeze, is why evenings cool off and why colonial officers called it a station they could stand. The weather is geography, not a personality trait.

q: Why is Vidhana Soudha stone, not concrete?
a: Kengal Hanumanthaiah, who pushed the 1950s building through, wanted a legislature that would last like a temple, not a bungalow. Granite and porphyry were the brief. The result is still the largest legislative building in India, and it reads as a palace because it was meant to.

q: Is Mysore pak actually from the palace?
a: Yes, in the useful sense. Around 1935, Kakasura Madappa, a cook in the Mysore palace, is credited with a ghee-besan-sugar sweet made for Krishna Raja Wadiyar IV. The 'pak' is the sugar-syrup stage. Palace kitchens, not a 21st-century brand, are the origin story.

Jacaranda is South American. It was planted here in the colonial gardening era and now defines a few late-spring streets. The pink avenue trumpets (Tabebuia) are guests too. Garden city was a planting project, not a forest that happened to be purple.

Basava is the bull, gudi is the temple. The neighbourhood is named for Dodda Basavana Gudi, the 16th-century Nandi that Kadlekai Parishe still orients around. A lot of pete names are still this literal if you read them in Kannada.

q: What is that temple-spire edge on an Ilkal saree?
a: Tope Teni is the pallu weaving: red, white and gold triangles that read as a row of temple towers. Ilkal (Bagalkot belt) is a GI-tagged Karnataka weave, not a generic 'south silk'. The teni is how you spot one without a label.

q: Is Dasara only the palace procession?
a: Jamboo Savari is the public postcard. In the same ten days, Mysuru households build gombe mane - stepped dolls and figurines - and invite neighbours in. Gombe Habba is Dasara at domestic scale, which is how most families actually mark it.

q: Pensioner's paradise, garden city, Silicon Valley - which stuck?
a: All three, in order of marketing eras. Cool weather and parks made a retirement station; Lalbagh and the lakes made 'garden city'; software parks from the 1990s made the Silicon Valley tag. The older names are still true on a weekday evening. The newest one is a district, not the whole map.

q: Why is a traffic junction called Silk Board?
a: It sits by the Central Silk Board / Karnataka silk-industry campus, not because anyone holds a board meeting in the flyover. Bengaluru's silk story is real - mulberry, Tipu-era encouragement, later mills - but the junction is named for the office next to it. You will still be late.
